head: Give space heaters 3 feet.
cap:
This time of year we run a lot of these.

Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from a space heater. Plug it straight into the wall, not a power strip, and shut it off when you leave the room or go to bed.

Space heaters are involved in most home heating fire deaths, per NFPA.

head: Get the chimney checked before the first fire.
cap:
Before you light the first fire of the season, have the chimney cleaned and inspected. NFPA says once a year.

Creosote builds up every time you burn, and it's what catches.

head: No CO alarm? Get one.
cap:
Furnaces, fireplaces, generators and gas stoves all run harder this time of year.

Put a carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area and on every level, and test it when you test the smoke alarms.

head: Heaters plug into the wall. Period.
cap:
Space heaters pull a lot of power. Extension cords and power strips aren't built for it.

One heater, one wall outlet. If the cord or plug gets hot, stop using it.

head: Grease fire? Lid on. Burner off.
cap:
Never put water on a grease fire.

Slide a lid over the pan, turn off the burner, and leave it covered until it cools. If it's spreading, get out and call 911.

head: Frying the turkey? Do it outside. Far from the house.
cap:
Thanksgiving week.

If you're frying, set up outside, well away from the house, garage and deck. Thaw the bird all the way and dry it, don't overfill the oil, and never leave it unattended.

head: Tomorrow is the busiest day of the year for kitchen fires.
cap:
Thanksgiving is the #1 day for home cooking fires. NFPA counted about 1,446 on Thanksgiving 2023, close to 4 times a normal day.

Stay in the kitchen while things are on the stove, keep kids 3 feet back, and keep a lid handy.

head: Test your smoke alarms before the holidays.
cap:
Push the button. If it doesn't sound, change the battery or replace the alarm. Alarms older than 10 years should be replaced.

Takes a minute. Do it before the house fills up with family.

head: Water the tree. Every day.
cap:
A dry Christmas tree can go up in seconds. In a CPSC test burn, a dried-out tree flashed the room in under a minute.

Water it every day, keep it 3 feet from heat sources, and get rid of it when the needles start dropping.

head: Check the lights before they go up.
cap:
Toss any strand with frayed wires, cracked sockets or loose connections. Lights and wiring are involved in about 2 of every 5 Christmas tree fires, per NFPA.

Turn them off before bed or when you leave.

head: Christmas is the #1 day for candle fires.
cap:
In 3 of every 5 home candle fires, something that could burn was too close to the candle (NFPA).

Keep candles 12 inches from anything that burns, and blow them out before you leave the room or go to sleep.

head: Clean the lint trap. Every load.
cap:
Dryers run hard all winter.

Clean the lint filter before or after every load, and check the vent hose behind the dryer for lint and kinks. Failure to clean is the leading factor in dryer fires, and they peak in January, per USFA.

head: Generators stay outside. 20 feet out.
cap:
Winter storm, power's out, the generator comes out.

Run it outside only, at least 20 feet from the house. Never in the garage, basement, shed or on the porch, and opening a door or window won't vent it.

CPSC estimates about 85 people die every year from CO from portable generators.

head: Hydrant out front? Dig it out.
cap:
After a snow, the plow buries the hydrant on your street.

If there's one near your house, shovel it out all the way around and clear a path to the road. If we have to dig for it, we're losing time.

Adopt the one on your block.

head: Two ways out of every room.
cap:
Family's home for the holidays. Good time to walk the escape plan.

Find 2 ways out of every room and pick a meeting spot out front. USFA says you may have less than 2 minutes to get out once the smoke alarm sounds.

Push the test button and run it once with everybody.

head: Ashes go in a metal can. Outside.
cap:
Ashes hold heat a lot longer than people think.

Put them in a metal container with a lid and set it outside, at least 10 feet from the house (USFA). Not in a paper bag, not in the garage, not on the deck.

head: Don't let the tree block the way out.
cap:
Tree, presents, extra chairs, coats piled by the door.

Keep the tree at least 3 feet from any heat source and make sure it isn't blocking an exit. More than 1 in 5 Christmas tree fires start with a heat source too close to the tree, per USFA.

Walk your way out tonight.

head: New gadgets? Charge them right.
cap:
A lot of lithium-ion batteries go under the tree this week. E-bikes, scooters, phones, toys.

Use the charger that came with it, unplug it when it's done, and don't charge it while you sleep (CPSC). If a battery gets hot, swells or smells, stop using it.

head: Merry Christmas from the firehouse.
cap:
Some of us are on shift today. That's the job.

If you're cooking, stay in the kitchen while anything's on the stove. Unattended cooking is the leading cause of kitchen fires, per NFPA.

Blow out the candles before bed. Merry Christmas.

head: Get the tree out of the house.
cap:
Christmas is over and that tree is drying out by the day.

NFPA says more than a third of home Christmas tree fires happen in January. Take it down, use your town's tree recycling, and don't leave it in the garage or up against the house.

head: Sparklers burn over 2,000 degrees.
cap:
New Year's Eve tomorrow. The sparklers come out.

They burn at more than 2,000 degrees, per CPSC. Keep them away from kids, keep a bucket of water close and drop the used ones in it.

Be safe out there.
